# Legumes fix nitrogen from the air (root nodule bacteria) (`nitrogen_fixation_biology`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: helped by legumes_green_manure, crop_rotation, microorganisms, photosynthesis_plant_nutrition
- Core idea: Grain crops take their nitrogen, the nutrient that most limits yield, from the soil and exhaust it. Peas, beans, lentils, vetch, clover and lucerne carry small swellings on their roots filled with bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and pass it to the plant. A legume crop therefore grows on poor soil and leaves it richer, most of all if it is grazed or ploughed in green rather than carried off. Working nodules are pink inside when cut. If a legume new to a district grows poorly and has no nodules, scatter soil from a field where it thrives, or coat the seed in a slurry of that soil. Free-living microbes and lightning also fix nitrogen; decomposition recycles nitrogen already present in manure and plant remains.
- Pitfalls:
  - Supposing all plants can do this, or that legume leaves absorb nitrogen directly
  - Harvesting the whole crop and expecting the field to be enriched; most of the nitrogen leaves with the seed and hay
  - Taking the nodules for a disease and selecting against them
  - Using soil from the wrong legume; each group has its own bacteria
  - Heavy manuring of the legume, which makes the plant stop feeding its nodules
- History: greece: c. 300 BC – Theophrastus notes that beans renew the soil; rome: 2nd c. BC – 1st c. AD – Cato, Varro and Columella recommend lupins, beans and vetch ploughed in; china: 1st c. BC – Fan Shengzhi's manual; c. 540 Qimin yaoshu ranks green manures and rotations with beans; americas: from c. 1000 BC – maize grown together with beans in Mesoamerica; europe: 1838 – Boussingault shows legumes gain nitrogen that cereals do not; 1886–1888 Hellriegel and Wilfarth prove the nodules do it; 1888 Beijerinck isolates the bacteria; 1890 Winogradsky isolates nitrifying bacteria; 1896 Nobbe and Hiltner sell cultures for inoculating seed
- Read:
  - Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth, Untersuchungen über die Stickstoffnahrung der Gramineen und Leguminosen (1888)
  - G. J. Leigh, The World's Greatest Fix: A History of Nitrogen and Agriculture (2004)
  - Vaclav Smil, Enriching the Earth: Fritz Haber, Carl Bosch, and the Transformation of World Food Production (2001)
